title: Frosty China welcome likely for Japan PM due to Taiwan row

 Tomohiro OSAKI Mon, 16 November 2026 at 7:58 am UTC 4 min read Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is headed for China, but may not get a warm welcome (Rie KIKUCHI) A brief, unsmiling handshake could be all Japanese premier Sanae Takaichi gets from President Xi Jinping this week during her first trip to China, with her remarks on Taiwan last year still rankling Beijing.
 The conservative Japanese leaderwill likely be denied a formal one-on-one meeting with Xi at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting in Shenzhen, analysts say.
 Takaichi is forecast to become the only leader of a major economy not to get a sit-down with Xi, Kyodo News reported citing Chinese sources.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Ties between the major Asian powers have deteriorated to historic lows after Takaichi suggested last year that Tokyo could intervene militarily if Beijing sought to take Taiwan by force.
 A furious China, which views the democratic island as part of its territory, retaliated with trade restrictions and warned its citizens not to travel to Japan.
 Trump reportedly sought to take on a peacemaker role in the dispute, subtly advising Takaichi to avoid provoking Beijing when it comes to Taiwan, the Wall Street Journal said last year.
 Xi-Takaichi talks at this week's summit are "highly unlikely unless the Japanese side signals that Prime Minister Takaichi is willing to say something akin to an apology," Bonnie Glaser, managing director of the Indo-Pacific program at Washington-based think tank German Marshall Fund, told AFP.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "Beijing has so far signalled it is unwilling to work with Japan on any issues until the Japanese side takes steps to address China's concerns about Takaichi's statement," she said.
 - Signs of detente -
 On Monday, Takaichi didn't name Xi as she listed world leaders she planned to hold talks with on the sidelines of APEC, which will mark her first visit to China as premier.
 But while high-level intergovernmental dialogue has largely stalled, signs of detente have emerged with Beijing accepting visits by individual Japanese lawmakers.
 When Chinese top diplomat Wang Yi met ex-foreign minister Takeshi Iwaya in September, Beijing issued a statement demanding the "correction" of Takaichi's Taiwan comment -- a watering-down from its earlier public calls for "retraction".
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Behind the softening is mostly the toll that strained ties are taking on China's economy, Akio Takahara, a visiting professor at Tokyo Woman's Christian University, told AFP.
 "Beijing is realising that its (hardline) stance has gone nowhere, that it is only hurting its economy with more Japanese firms retreating," the Chinese studies expert said.
 "I think that's why Xi has started sending some signals," he said.
 The ball is now believed to be in Japan's court -- except the Takaichi leadership has shown no inclination to return it.
 That represents a stark contrast from the APEC Beijing summit in 2014, where Xi's talks with then-prime minister Shinzo Abe -- following a stiff handshake -- materialised after months of painstaking diplomatic negotiation.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement That landmark meeting improved ties frozen by Abe's surprise visit in 2013 to a controversial Tokyo shrine honouring Japan's war dead, as well as the preceding administration's nationalisation of disputed islands also claimed by China.
 But this time around, while Takaichi's official line is to remain "always open to dialogue" with China, there seems to be little desire to secure a head-to-head with Xi, experts say.
 Emboldened by rock-solid support from her conservative base, Takaichi has adopted a "staunchly anti-Chinese, overtly pro-Taiwan approach" rarely seen in previous administrations, Noriyuki Kawamura, a professor emeritus at Nagoya University of Foreign Studies, told AFP.
 Although a snub by Xi risks embarrassing Takaichi, "it would also allow her to impress on her anti-China voters how badly she was treated, and potentially further fuel their support," the expert in Japan-China relations said.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement - Reputational risk -
 Still, Beijing is adamant that Japan must budge.
 China's Wang ignored Japanese foreign minister Toshimitsu Motegi on the sidelines of an ASEAN conference in July, strolling past him "without so much as a glance", according to the Yomiuri newspaper.
 Motegi later framed the encounter as a "brief greeting" with Wang, but Beijing denied any exchange took place.
 For Takaichi to return the ball, China needs to send "more obvious signs" of rapprochement, such as releasing a pair of arrested Japanese businessmen suspected of smuggling banned items, professor Takahara said.
 However, Takaichi getting cold-shouldered by Xi risks marring Japan's regional reputation, Kawamura warns.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "It would make it obvious to Asian countries that Japan-China relations are now a destabilising factor in East Asia" and that "Japan's power in diplomacy with China is declining", he said.
 Kawamura expects that the two leaders will at least exchange a "cold" and "expressionless" handshake.
 Denying her even that would contradict China's aspect as "a country that has historically valued etiquette", Kawamura said.
 "If even that doesn't happen, that would be tragic -- proof that Japan-China diplomacy has severely gone off the rails."
